III p163.text: Against the suffering of sensuous nature the human heart has only recourse to its moral nature as counterpoise. It is, therefore, necessary, in order to stimulate this in a more pressing manner, for the tragic poet to prolong the torments of sense, but he must also give a glimpse to the latter of the satisfaction of its wants, so as to render the victory of the moral sense so much the more difficult and glorious.

research_update: A separate research reader checked both places against German Maltzahn 1879 pp. 163–164 and the Dole 1902 inner volume II pp. 82–83, as well as Bell 1875 p. 358. English agrees with print and generally follows the original; in p163 glimpse and wants add nuances and the rendering of Sittlichkeit varies, while p164 charm our souls expands the German.
